name: Treaty with the Snake, 1865
aka: Treaty with the Woll-pah-pe tribe of Snake Indians
nations: Woll-pah-pe band of Northern Paiute (Snake); descendants among the Klamath Tribes and other Northern Paiute nations
promises: Article 2: the Woll-pah-pe ceded the country between the north fork of John Day's River, Crooked River, Harney Lake and the heads of the Malheur and Burnt rivers.
Article 3: the band to move to the Klamath reservation set by the treaty of October 1864, under the protection of an agent.
Article 4: depredations against band members to be punished as if committed against white persons.
Articles 6 and 7: $5,000 to fence, break and cultivate land in the first year, then $2,000 a year for five years and $1,200 a year for ten years.
today: The Indian Claims Commission in Docket 17 (Snake or Piute Indians of the former Malheur Reservation) found that the Woll-pah-pe cession overlapped the 1855 Walla Walla and 1864 Klamath cessions and part of the later Malheur Reservation; it did not find a breach of this treaty.

openQuestions: Whether the annuities in Articles 6 and 7 were paid, and whether the band ever settled at Klamath, was not traced.
treaties.json gives the Klamath Tribes as sole present-day tribe; the OSU database lists many Shoshone and Paiute successors. Which nation carries this band today was not settled.
The Klamath Tribes' history page names the Yahooskin band but not the 1865 treaty.
Royce (p. 837) notes area 474 conflicts with the 1855 Walla Walla and Middle Oregon cessions and the 1864 Klamath cession.

2026-11-08 sweep: Court of Claims and ICC full text searched for snake, Walpapi, Woll-pah-pe and August 12 1865; in Northern Paiute Nation v. United States, Docket 87 (7 Ind. Cl. Comm. 322, March 24, 1959) the Commission found the Walpapi a separate land-using entity, noted the band was treated with and moved to Klamath, and excluded its area because no claim on this treaty (for unconscionable consideration) had been pleaded. No finding on this treaty. Status unchanged.
